Domain skills and interaction skills stay in this repo. # Browser Harness ♞ Browser Harness lets Claude Code, Codex or Cursor use your real Chrome browser: open pages, click, type, read and download, logged in as you. Paste one prompt into your coding agent to set it up. It talks to Chrome over the DevTools Protocol (CDP), and the agent writes any missing helper as it works, so the harness gets better with each task. Open source, MIT licensed. Try browser-harness in [Browser Use Cloud](https://cloud.browser-use.com/v4?utm_campaign=browser-harness-use-in-cloud&utm_source=github) or paste the setup prompt into your coding agent. ``` ● agent: wants to upload a file │ ● agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py → helper missing │ ● agent writes it agent_helpers.py │ + custom helper ✓ file uploaded ``` **You will never use the browser again.** ## See it work **Task:** "Open my X profile, find my latest 20 video posts, and download them." [![Download my latest 20 X videos](docs/download-latest-20-x-videos.gif)](https://browser-use.com/showcase/videos/download-latest-20-x-videos.mp4) ## Setup prompt Paste into Claude Code or Codex (Cursor: use the [MCP config](#cursor) below): ```text Install browser-use with `uv tool install browser-use`, run `browser-use skill install` to register the skill, and connect it to my browser. If setup or connection fails, run `browser-use --doctor` and follow its output and the error message. ``` The agent will open `chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging`. On first setup, tick the checkbox so the agent can connect to your browser: ## How it works - [`install.md`](install.md) connects the agent to your browser. - [`SKILL.md`](SKILL.md) teaches it the browser workflow. - [`src/browser_harness/`](src/browser_harness/) stays protected while the agent writes reusable helpers in its local workspace. ## Compared with other browser tools | | Works with | Browser it drives | What you approve in your own Chrome | |---|---|---|---| | **Browser Harness** | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, any MCP client via `browser-harness-mcp` | Your running Chrome, logged in as you | Whole browser: on Chrome 144+, tick remote debugging in `chrome://inspect`, then click Allow | | **Playwright MCP** | Any MCP client (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot and more) | Its own browser profile by default. Your Chrome with `--extension` (Playwright Extension) or `--cdp-endpoint` | Chosen tabs (one tab group per client) via the extension, approval skippable with a token; or whole browser via `--cdp-endpoint` | | **Playwright CLI** | Claude Code, GitHub Copilot and other agents that run shell commands | Its own browser by default. Your Chrome with `attach --extension=chrome` or `attach --cdp=chrome` | Chosen tab via the Playwright Extension, or whole browser via `--cdp` | | **Chrome DevTools MCP** | Any MCP client (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Antigravity and more), plus a CLI | A new Chrome with a dedicated profile by default. Your Chrome 144+ with `--autoConnect` | Whole browser: the same Chrome 144+ toggle and Allow dialog; the server sees every open window of that profile | | **agent-browser** | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot and more, as a CLI with a skill, plus an MCP server | Its own Chrome for Testing by default. A copy of your Chrome profile with `--profile`. Your running Chrome with `--auto-connect` or `--cdp` | Whole browser via `--auto-connect` or `--cdp`: the same Chrome 144+ toggle and Allow dialog | | **Claude in Chrome** | Claude Code (CLI or VS Code) with the Claude extension, signed in with a direct Anthropic plan (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise), not an API key | Your Chrome, Edge or other Chromium browser, logged in as you | Per site: allow sites in the extension, or per action in Claude Code (auto mode can skip the per-site check). Claude works in a tab group it opens | | **ChatGPT Browser and browser extension** | Codex and ChatGPT chats in the ChatGPT desktop app, not Codex CLI or the Codex IDE extension | Browser: a separate profile. Extension: your Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera or Vivaldi profile | Per site: asks before each new website (allow once, for this site, or for all sites) | Matched eval by Browser Use on 100 of the 200 public [BU Bench V2.1](https://github.com/browser-use/benchmark) tasks (bu2-001 to bu2-100; 101-200 not run). Measured 2026-10-14. - Same agent for every tool: Codex CLI 0.144.6, GPT-6 Luna, medium reasoning, web search off. Same frozen judge. - Browser Harness was given to the agent as its CLI and SKILL.md, not `browser-harness-mcp`. Playwright MCP and Chrome DevTools MCP ran as MCP servers with default settings. agent-browser ran as its CLI and skill. - Every tool drove the same fresh Browser Use cloud browser over CDP. This does not measure each tool's default or local-Chrome mode. - One run per task. Agent failures were never retried. Runner, browser and judge failures were rerun once (Browser Harness 3 tasks, Playwright MCP 4, Chrome DevTools MCP 6, agent-browser 0). | Tool | Mean rubric score 0-100 (95% CI) | Fully solved | Median input tokens per task | Median model cost per task (GPT-6 Luna list price) | Median agent time per task | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Browser Harness a6426f84 (main) | 60.4 (55.2-65.4) | 11% | 2.1M | $0.042 | 9.0 min | | Playwright MCP 0.0.83 | 60.0 (55.1-65.0) | 11% | 4.4M | $0.066 | 8.3 min | | Chrome DevTools MCP 1.10.1 | 61.0 (55.8-65.9) | 11% | 6.7M | $0.097 | 8.7 min | | agent-browser 0.39.1 | 56.3 (51.1-61.5) | 9% | 3.3M | $0.056 | 11.2 min | No tool wins on score: every paired difference against Browser Harness has a 95% CI that includes zero (other tool minus Browser Harness: agent-browser -4.0, CI -10.0 to +1.8; Playwright MCP -0.4, -6.6 to +5.7; Chrome DevTools MCP +0.6, -5.6 to +6.6). It was slower than Playwright MCP and Chrome DevTools MCP (median 9.0 vs 8.3 and 8.7 min) and faster than agent-browser (11.2 min). These are medians, with no confidence intervals. A first agent-browser run was discarded: a setup bug on our side let it launch its own local browser instead of the shared cloud browser. The row shows the corrected rerun. Measured with Codex only. Claude Code, Cursor, Playwright CLI and Claude in Chrome were not measured. Method and per-task scores: [coding-agent-browser-tools.json](https://browser-use.com/benchmarks/coding-agent-browser-tools.json). ### When to use something else - **Playwright** (Test, MCP or CLI): isolated, repeatable CI tests of your own app, in a clean browser with no personal logins. - **Chrome DevTools MCP**: performance traces and DevTools debugging (network, console, source-mapped stack traces). - **Claude in Chrome**: you only use Claude and have a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan. - **Cursor's built-in Browser**: the agent doesn't need your logged-in Chrome. It runs in its own per-workspace profile. OpenAI's Codex labels its browser feature "Browser use" in its settings. It is separate from Browser Use, the company behind this repo. ## Scale with Browser Use Cloud Use your local browser for logged-in, personal work. When you want many browsers in parallel, with live previews, proxies, stealth, CAPTCHA solving, and more, scale with [Browser Use Cloud](https://cloud.browser-use.com/new-api-key). ## MCP server `browser-use --cli-mcp` exposes the browser control helpers as MCP tools over stdio, so any MCP client (Claude Code, Devin, Cursor, etc.) can drive the browser without writing a second CDP layer. The older `browser-harness-mcp` keeps working; see [docs/MCP.md](docs/MCP.md). ### Cursor Add this to `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project, or to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project. repo.readme:
Easy, fast, and cheap LLM serving for everyone

| Documentation | Blog | Paper | Twitter/X | User Forum | Developer Slack |

🔥 We have built a vLLM website to help you get started with vLLM. Please visit [vllm.ai](https://vllm.ai) to learn more. For events, please visit [vllm.ai/events](https://vllm.ai/events) to join us. --- ## About vLLM is a fast and easy-to-use library for LLM inference and serving. Originally developed in the [Sky Computing Lab](https://sky.cs.berkeley.edu) at UC Berkeley, vLLM has grown into one of the most active open-source AI projects built and maintained by a diverse community of many dozens of academic institutions and companies from over 2000 contributors. vLLM is fast with: - State-of-the-art serving throughput - Efficient management of attention key and value memory with [**PagedAttention**](https://blog.vllm.ai/2023/06/20/vllm.html) - Continuous batching of incoming requests, chunked prefill, prefix caching - Fast and flexible model execution with piecewise and full CUDA/HIP graphs - Quantization: FP8, MXFP8/MXFP4, NVFP4, INT8, INT4, GPTQ/AWQ, GGUF, compressed-tensors, ModelOpt, TorchAO, and [more](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/quantization/index.html) - Optimized attention kernels including FlashAttention, FlashInfer, TRTLLM-GEN, FlashMLA, and Triton - Optimized GEMM/MoE kernels for various precisions using CUTLASS, TRTLLM-GEN, CuTeDSL - Speculative decoding including n-gram, suffix, EAGLE, DFlash - Automatic kernel generation and graph-level transformations using torch.compile - Disaggregated prefill, decode, and encode vLLM is flexible and easy to use with: - Seamless integration with popular Hugging Face models - High-throughput serving with various decoding algorithms, including *parallel sampling*, *beam search*, and more - Tensor, pipeline, data, expert, and context parallelism for distributed inference - Streaming outputs - Generation of structured outputs using xgrammar or guidance - Tool calling and reasoning parsers - OpenAI-compatible API server, plus Anthropic Messages API and gRPC support - Efficient multi-LoRA support for dense and MoE layers - Support for NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Intel GPUs, and x86/ARM/PowerPC CPUs. Additionally, diverse hardware plugins such as Google TPUs, Intel Gaudi, IBM Spyre, Huawei Ascend, Rebellions NPU, Apple Silicon, MetaX GPU, Iluvatar CoreX GPU, and more. vLLM seamlessly supports 200+ model architectures on Hugging Face, including: - Decoder-only LLMs (e.g., Llama, Qwen, Gemma) - Mixture-of-Expert LLMs (e.g., Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-MoE, GPT-OSS) - Hybrid attention and state-space models (e.g., Mamba, Qwen3.5) - Multi-modal models (e.g., LLaVA, Qwen-VL, Pixtral) - Embedding and retrieval models (e.g., E5-Mistral, GTE, ColBERT) - Reward and classification models (e.g., Qwen-Math) Find the full list of supported models [here](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/models/supported_models.html). ## Getting Started Install vLLM with [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) (recommended) or `pip`: ```bash uv pip install vllm vllm download-kernels # precompiled kernels for faster startup ``` Or [build from source](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/getting_started/installation/gpu/index.html#build-wheel-from-source) for development. Visit our [documentation](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/) to learn more. - [Installation](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/getting_started/installation.html) - [Quickstart](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/getting_started/quickstart.html) - [List of Supported Models](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/models/supported_models.html) ## Contributing We welcome and value any contributions and collaborations. Please check out [Contributing to vLLM](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/contributing/index.html) for how to get involved. ## Citation If you use vLLM for your research, please cite our [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180): ```bibtex @inproceedings{kwon2023efficient, title={Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention}, author={Woosuk Kwon and Zhuohan Li and Siyuan Zhuang and Ying Sheng and Lianmin Zheng and Cody Hao Yu and Joseph E. Gonzalez and Hao Zhang and Ion Stoica}, booktitle={Proceedings of the ACM SIGOPS 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles}, year={2023} } ``` ## Contact Us - For technical questions and feature requests, please use GitHub [Issues](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues) - For discussing with fellow users, please use the [vLLM Forum](https://discuss.vllm.ai) - For coordinating contributions and development, please use [Slack](https://slack.vllm.ai) - For security disclosures, please use GitHub's [Security Advisories](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/security/advisories) feature - For collaborations and partnerships, please contact us at [collaboration@vllm.ai](mailto:collaboration@vllm.ai) ## Media Kit - If you wish to use vLLM's logo, please refer to [our media kit repo](https://github.com/vllm-project/media-kit)

# v0.34.0 **1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new).** Thank you! ## TL;DR - **10 new models** (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!) - **Extensible KV cache is on by default:** vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now **remove `gpu_memory_utilization`** from your configs. - **Model Runner V1 is gone.** Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner. - **Big speedups** on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3). - **Upgrade check:** default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and `huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0` is required. See [Before you upgrade](#before-you-upgrade). ## Before you upgrade > [!IMPORTANT] > These changes can break existing setups. | Change | What to do | PR | |---|---|---| | Model Runner V1 removed | Remove `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0`; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to `vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor`. | #63373 | | Default `--block-size` is 64 (was 16) | Pass `--block-size 16` to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. | #63231 | | Extensible KV cache on by default; `gpu_memory_utilization` defaults to 1.0 | **In most cases it's now best to not set `gpu_memory_utilization`**. This should provide maximum kv cache capacity while avoiding runtime OOMs. Use it to share a GPU with other processes or when extensible kv cache is disabled. | #56492 | | ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped | Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. `-rocm72` is no longer published. | #61939 | | `huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0` required | Also requires `tokenizers >= 0.23.3` and `timm >= 1.0.30`. | #64779 | | QuTLASS / `fp_quant` removed | `fp_quant` checkpoints no longer load. | #65230 | | Marlin W4A8 removed | Use `--quantization humming` with `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` instead of `VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE`. | #65542 | | Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed | — | #64287 | All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in [the full changelog](#full-changelog). ## New models | Model | Notes | PR | |---|---|---| | **Mistral Large 4** | 1T total / 52B active, FP8 and NVFP4. Runs on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350. | #64534 | | MiniMax-M3.1-Flash | Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft | #64111 | | NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe | 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and `/v1/audio/transcriptions` | #64282 | | Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview | BF16 and NVFP4, `ripple` reasoning and tool parsers | #65745 | | Zyphra ZAYA1 | ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview | #65302 | | Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 | DASH sparse attention | #64016 | | Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio | | #65826, #65827, #65828 | | NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 | ASR and X↔En translation | #64215 | | Ming3-ASR | | #63585 | | NVIDIA Parakeet TDT | Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin | #65005 | ## Highlights ### Extensible KV cache, on by default - On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free **after** CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492). - **Result:** a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency. - **Trade-off:** per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.9` or `--no-enable-extensible-kv-cache`. - Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674). ### Model Runner V2 only - Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373). - Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464). ### Speculative decoding - **Suffix decoding** runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339). - **Custom speculators:** declarative configs plus a `register_speculative_method` plugin API (#63205). - **CUDA graphs** for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989). - **Adaptive verification** works with XPress (#65175). - **Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype**, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198). ### Performance | Improvement | Hardware | Gain | PR | |---|---|---|---| | Step5 NVFP4 MoE on TRTLLM-Gen | 4×GB200 | up to **1.95×** decode | #65152 | | GLM-5.3-Flash DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE | NVIDIA | **1.6×** output throughput vs DEP4 | #60895 | | Muse Spark Open specialized decode (opt-in) | GB300 | **1.5×** single-stream decode | #64077 | | Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (default) | GB200 | GLM-5.3 TTFT **1.24–1.40×** faster at 32K–128K | #63956 | | KV-balanced MLA decode for Kimi-K3 (opt-in) | GB300 | **1.34–1.59×** decode attention | #63638 | | Qwen3.5 on breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) | NVIDIA | **3.0–8.8%** lower decode ITL | #51012 | | FlyDSL decode monokernel, Muse Spark Open DSpark | 8×MI355X | **+35–57%** interactivity at conc. 1–8 | #63440 | ### AMD ROCm - Release images and wheels are **ROCm 10.0 only** (#61939). - MoRI EPv2 via `--all2all-backend mori` (#61361). - Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435). - TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418). ### Serving and operations - **Checkpoint/restore** (CRIU + `cuda-checkpoint`) through `/checkpoint/prepare`, `/checkpoint/status` and `/checkpoint/restore`, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570). - **Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down:** dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370). - Best-effort **NUMA binding** on by default (#61258). - Opt-in **cache-aware admission** ordering (#54625). - Rust frontend: stateless **Responses API** (#63902) and **`n > 1`** (#65625). ## Install **Python wheels** | Platform | Install | |---|---| | CUDA 13.0 (PyPI) | `pip install vllm` | | CUDA 13.0 (uv) | `uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto` | | ROCm 10.0 | `pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.34.0/rocm100` | | XPU | `uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/0.34.0/xpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu --index-strategy unsafe-best-match` | **Docker images** | Platform | Image | Short alias | |---|---|---| | CUDA 13.0 (default) | `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0` | | CUDA 13.0 + DeepEP over AWS EFA | `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0-efa` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-efa` | | ROCm 10.0 | `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-rocm` | | CPU | `vllm/vllm-openai-cpu:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-cpu` | | XPU | `vllm/vllm-openai-xpu:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-xpu` | `latest` tags work the same way (e.g. `vllm/vllm:latest-rocm`). The default CUDA image now includes the AWS EFA userspace (libfabric, aws-ofi-nccl). The `-efa` image adds DeepEP built for EFA and routes NCCL over EFA by default (#65576). The **Assets** section below has the source tarball and the CUDA 13.0 (x86_64, arm64), CPU (x86_64, arm64, macOS) and XPU (x86_64) wheels. ## Full changelog
Model support - **Mistral Large 4** (#64534) runs on MRV2 with: - sparse MLA plus the DSA indexer, and cross-layer KV sharing; - DSpark, DCP/PCP, NIXL P/D and HiSparse. - **Other new models:** - MiniMax-M3.1-Flash (#64111), plus P/D across different prefill and decode TP (#64475). - Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe with MTP and DFlash2 (#64282, #64944). - **DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1** - Prefill gathers compressed KV once per KV-source group: 38 → 4 gathers per step (#59131). - Decoder replay graphs share the model graph pool: prefill graph memory 15.52 → 9.88 GiB per rank on GB200 (#63155). - `fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant` 3.5× faster, prefill 6% faster (#63540). - DSpark/MTP memory savings of about 512 MiB per GPU (#63996). - Engram host tables shared across DP ranks (#62359). - DeepGEMM sparse MQA logits on the FP8 indexer cache (#62011). - Packed multi-image vision encoding, 1.6–2.6× (#65030). - LoRA on the language model, compressor and `wo_a` layers (#57245, #64880). - DSpark with PCP (#61994); PCP with PP or DP (#63098). - Fixes: sparse prefill in FULL CUDA graphs (#59986), prefill memory budgeting (#63047), MTP embedding under PP (#65816), DeepSeek-V3.2 PP (#59961). - **GLM** - GLM-5.3-Flash: DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE (#60895), adaptive verification (#60229), row-strided QKV into FlashKDA (#61614). - GLM-5.3 FP8 MoE sorted-A TMA on H200, 6.0–7.6% E2E throughput (#64760). - FP8 KV cache for DSpark and DFlash drafts (#63841, #64612, #65553). - FP32 indexer MQA logits restored for GLM-5/GLM-5.3/HY-V4, with new `--attention-config.indexer_logits_dtype` (#64580). - Fused KDA convs fix stale weights after RL refit (#60991). - **Muse Spark** - Opt-in Muse Spark Open specialized decode on GB300 (#64077). - One RoPE cache shared across layers: 11.5 GiB per GPU saved, 14.5% more KV cache on 8×B200 (#65206). - GEMM and communication+norm fusions (#65438, #64638); hybrid DeepGEMM MegaMoE / TRT-LLM for NVFP4 (#64525). - CUDA routing kernel (#64553), MegaMoE JIT warmup (#63920), DSpark draft loading fix (#65125). - **MiniMax-M3 / M3.1** - Sequence parallelism and GEMM-RS for TP + MegaMoE, 14–20% lower P50 TTFT (#64659), also with PP (#65537). - Fused norm + MXFP8 quant, 1.39–1.60× (#64852). - Triton query-tiled sparse prefill on Hopper (#57420); SM90 split-K indexer (#64037). - No host sync in prefill metadata (#65883); NVFP4 MegaMoE warmup (#66227); fmha_sm100 indexer updates (#66228). - Fixes: M3.1 prefill workspace (#64856), sequence parallelism (#65496), encoder CUDA graphs (#65226). - **Kimi** - Opt-in `--attention-backend KIMI_K3_KV_BALANCED_MLA` for agentic workloads on Blackwell (#63638). - Kimi-K3 MegaMoE symmetric buffer 10.73 → 2.50 GiB per GPU at TP8 EP (#63541). - FlashInfer fused FP8 chunked-context K/V pack (#61527). - Fixes: KDA prefill OOM (#63989), NaNs via FlashKDA/FlashMLA pins (#64759), sleep mode (#64583, #66273). - Kimi K3.1 groundwork landed (#66030, #66028), but **K3.1 is not servable in this release**. - **Qwen** - Qwen3.5: breakable CUDA graphs instead of torch.compile (#51012); fused norm/gate + quant (#64509) and AR + norm + quant (#64723); GDN `in_proj` overlap (#64425, #64999). - GDN prefill state gather/scatter fused for Qwen3-Next/Qwen3.5 and Kimi KDA, 1.16–1.50× (#66064). - Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: PLE disk offload via `--engram-config '{"disk_offload": true}'` (27 GiB less on DGX Spark, #59958), PP (#60234), shared QSA top-k buffer (#65619), loading fixes (#62318, #65812, #64820, #60490). - Fixes: long-context int32 overflow (#63761), multi-layer MTP (#62111). - **Other models** - Step5 MegaMoE with PP (#65504) and KV block sizing (#65153). - Gemma 4: multimodal encoder DP (#60314), PP (#65989), FA4 FP8 MMA on SM90 (#60372). - Moved to the Transformers modeling backend: OLMoE (#63384), Gemma v1 and StableLM (#66393), Aria (#59767; temporarily about 11% less KV cache and 25% lower image throughput). - Matryoshka dimensions for EmbeddingGemma 2 (#64885, #60978); RADIO C-RADIO v2/v3/v4 (#58468). - Qwen3-ASR on the upstream Transformers config; no `--hf-overrides` needed for the ForceAligner (#66097, #63274). - Fixes: GPT-OSS MXFP4 LoRA (#65825), PLaMo3 GPTQ (#62836), Ling3 (#65088), DomynEdge (#66819). - **Multimodal** - Encoder CUDA graphs for Pixtral/Mistral3 (#56277), shared capture buffers (#65084), one replay per batch up to `encoder_cudagraph_max_token_budget` (#65227). - On-device input normalization for Nemotron VL (#57924), Gemma 3 (#64487), Gemma 4 (#65577). - `--mm-encoder-tp-mode data` for MiMo-V2.6 (#64179). - Fixes: FlashInfer ViT attention on GLM-4.1V/GLM-OCR/GLM-5.3-Flash (#65778), Qwen3-Omni and Qwen2.5-Omni video budgets (#66017, #66190), dots_ocr with TP (#64543), embedding-only startup (#65689), media cache eviction (#65363).
Engine core - **Extensible KV cache** - On by default on CUDA and ROCm (#56492). - Headroom for measured allocator fragmentation, validated on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 at TP8+EP on 8×H200 (#67296). - Fixes: sizing and startup OOMs (#67485, #66523, #66731, #66197, #65554), connectors that failed to start (#65225), up to 84% undersized caches on DGX Spark (#65413), `--max-model-len auto` (#65463). - Startup warning when an explicit `gpu_memory_utilization` withholds memory from it (#66704); docs on when to set it (#67071). - **Model Runner V2** - The only runner after MRV1's removal (#63373); DBO with spec decode and DCP (#61464). - Separate prefill (token) and decode (request) CUDA graph capture sizes (#63406). - Staged writes copied straight into UVA (#63633); idle sampler writes skipped, about 10–11% faster small-batch decode (#62748). - Sampler warmed up after graph capture to stop memory growth under load (#62560). - Lower peak memory for chunked prompt logprobs (#64841, #64914); Triton ReplaySSM (#65033). - NVIDIA Confidential Computing decode fixes (#59981). - **Speculative decoding** - Suffix decoding (#60339) and custom speculators (#63205) on MRV2; draft-model CUDA graphs (#60989). - XPress with adaptive verification (#65175); adaptive verification draft budgets on a Triton kernel (#63421). - Batch-sharded draft logits (#63554); DSpark sequential blocks (#63886). - DSpark sliding-window MLA draft layers (#63795) under DCP (#63796); fused Markov sampling, 42–50% less sampling time (#64476); `draft_lm_head_quantization` (#64368). - Draft KV cache dtype aligned with the target (#65198). - Trace replay with ngram/EAGLE3/MTP, 1.47–2.03× (#63275); repo.readme: # OpenAI Agents SDK [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/openai-agents?label=pypi%20package)](https://pypi.org/project/openai-agents/) The OpenAI Agents SDK is a lightweight yet powerful framework for building multi-agent workflows. It is provider-agnostic, supporting the OpenAI Responses and Chat Completions APIs, as well as 100+ other LLMs. > [!NOTE] > Looking for the JavaScript/TypeScript version? Check out [Agents SDK JS/TS](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-js). ### Core concepts: 1. [**Agents**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/agents): LLMs configured with instructions, tools, guardrails, and handoffs 1. [**Sandbox agents**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/sandbox_agents): Agents preconfigured to work with a container to perform work over long time horizons. 1. [**Realtime agents**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/realtime/quickstart/): Build powerful voice agents with `gpt-realtime-2.1` and full agent features 1. [**Voice agents**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/voice/quickstart/): Build voice pipelines that combine speech-to-text, an agent workflow, and text-to-speech 1. **[Agents as tools](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tools/#agents-as-tools) / [Handoffs](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/handoffs/)**: Delegating to other agents for specific tasks 1. [**Tools**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tools/): Various Tools let agents take actions (functions, MCP, hosted tools) 1. [**Guardrails**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/guardrails/): Configurable safety checks for input and output validation 1. [**Human in the loop**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/human_in_the_loop/): Built-in mechanisms for involving humans across agent runs 1. [**Sessions**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/sessions/): Automatic conversation history management across agent runs 1. [**Tracing**](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/tracing/): Built-in tracking of agent runs, allowing you to view, debug and optimize your workflows Explore the [examples](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples) directory to see the SDK in action, and read our [documentation](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/) for more details. ## Get started To get started, set up your Python environment (Python 3.10 or newer required), and then install OpenAI Agents SDK package. ### venv ```bash python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install openai-agents ``` For voice support, install with the optional `voice` group: `pip install 'openai-agents[voice]'`. For Redis session support, install with the optional `redis` group: `pip install 'openai-agents[redis]'`. ### uv If you're familiar with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), installing the package would be even easier: ```bash uv init uv add openai-agents ``` For voice support, install with the optional `voice` group: `uv add 'openai-agents[voice]'`. For Redis session support, install with the optional `redis` group: `uv add 'openai-agents[redis]'`. ## Run your first agents The SDK supports four primary ways to run agents. Set the `OPENAI_API_KEY` environment variable before running any of these examples. ### Run a text agent Use a text `Agent` for workflows that do not need a persistent realtime connection or a sandbox workspace. ```python from agents import Agent, Runner agent = Agent(name="Assistant", instructions="You are a helpful assistant") result = Runner.run_sync(agent, "Write a haiku about recursion in programming.") print(result.final_output) # Code within the code, # Functions calling themselves, # Infinite loop's dance. ``` (_For Jupyter notebook users, see [hello_world_jupyter.ipynb](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/examples/basic/hello_world_jupyter.ipynb)_) ### Run a sandbox agent Use a [`SandboxAgent`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/sandbox_agents) when the agent needs to inspect files, run commands, apply patches, or preserve workspace state across longer tasks. This example uses `UnixLocalSandboxClient`, which is supported on macOS and Linux. On Windows, use `DockerSandboxClient` with the `openai-agents[docker]` extra or a hosted sandbox client instead; see [Sandbox clients](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/sandbox/clients/) for setup details. ```python from agents import Runner from agents.run import RunConfig from agents.sandbox import Manifest, SandboxAgent, SandboxRunConfig from agents.sandbox.entries import GitRepo from agents.sandbox.sandboxes import UnixLocalSandboxClient agent = SandboxAgent( name="Workspace Assistant", instructions="Inspect the sandbox workspace before answering.", default_manifest=Manifest( entries={"repo": GitRepo(repo="openai/openai-agents-python", ref="main")} ), ) result = Runner.run_sync( agent, "Inspect the repo README and summarize what this project does.", run_config=RunConfig(sandbox=SandboxRunConfig(client=UnixLocalSandboxClient())), ) print(result.final_output) ``` ### Run a realtime agent Use a [`RealtimeAgent`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/realtime/quickstart/) for low-latency, server-side voice and multimodal experiences over WebSocket. ```python import asyncio from agents.realtime import RealtimeAgent, RealtimeRunner async def main() -> None: agent = RealtimeAgent( name="Assistant", instructions="You are a helpful voice assistant. Keep responses short." ) runner = RealtimeRunner(starting_agent=agent) session = await runner.run() async with session: await session.send_message("Say hello in one short sentence.") async for event in session: if event.type == "audio": # Forward or play event.audio.data. pass elif event.type == "history_added": print(event.item) elif event.type == "agent_end": break if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) ``` ### Run a voice agent Use a [`VoicePipeline`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/voice/quickstart/) to turn audio into text, run an agent workflow, and stream generated speech. ```python import asyncio import numpy as np from agents import Agent from agents.voice import AudioInput, SingleAgentVoiceWorkflow, VoicePipeline async def main() -> None: agent = Agent(name="Assistant", instructions="You are a helpful voice assistant.") pipeline = VoicePipeline(workflow=SingleAgentVoiceWorkflow(agent)) audio_input = AudioInput(buffer=np.zeros(24000 * 3, dtype=np.int16)) result = await pipeline.run(audio_input) async for event in result.stream(): if event.type == "voice_stream_event_audio": # Forward or play event.data. pass if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) ``` Explore the [examples](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/tree/main/examples) directory to see the SDK in action, and read our [documentation](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/) for more details. ## Contributing Please share bug reports and feature requests through [GitHub issues](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/issues). Pull requests are limited to repository collaborators; we do not accept pull requests from non-collaborators. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for the contribution policy and development guide. For security vulnerabilities, follow [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/SECURITY.md). ## Acknowledgements We'd like to acknowledge the excellent work of the open-source community, especially: - [Pydantic](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/) - [Requests](https://github.com/psf/requests) - [MCP Python SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk) - [Griffe](https://github.com/mkdocstrings/griffe) This library has these optional dependencies: - [websockets](https://github.com/python-websockets/websockets) - [SQLAlchemy](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy) - [any-llm](https://github.com/mozilla-ai/any-llm) and [LiteLLM](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm) We also rely on the following tools to manage the project: - [uv](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv) and [ruff](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff) - [mypy](https://github.com/python/mypy) and [Pyright](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright) - [pytest](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest) and [Coverage.py](https://github.com/coveragepy/coveragepy) - [MkDocs](https://github.com/squidfunk/mkdocs-material) We're committed to continuing to build the Agents SDK as an open source framework so others in the community can expand on our approach.

## [0.25.0](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/compare/v0.24.0...v0.25.0) (2026-11-17)

## Key Changes

Version 0.25.0 removes the beta Runloop sandbox provider and changes how Pydantic run contexts are checkpointed. Runloop users should preserve their workspace data before switching providers. Applications that share checkpoints across workers should upgrade readers first.

### Highlights:

- Migrate Runloop workloads to another supported sandbox provider, such as Modal, or remain on 0.24.0 while migrating. Provider-specific sessions and snapshots require a separate data migration.
- Resume nested agent-tool approvals with output guardrails using RunState schema `1.22`. Pydantic checkpoints now preserve default values and in-place edits. Use a custom serializer for process-local resources.
- `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` now defaults to `gpt-6-luna`. Set `model="gpt-4.1"` to keep the previous choice. Agent model settings also follow the selected model more closely. Native Chat Completions tool requests for `gpt-6-sol` and `gpt-6-luna` default to non-reasoning mode when no effort is supplied.
- Runner handoffs can opt into recovery with `failure_error_function`. Omitting it preserves exception propagation. The demo REPL can now approve or reject individual tool calls.
- MCP v2 Streamable HTTP supports concurrent requests. MCP v1 retains serialized requests. Failed and incomplete Responses calls now retain provider-reported token usage.

repo.readme: > [!NOTE] > **Browser Harness is now the engine inside [Browser Use](https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use).** Use the `browser-use` CLI: same helpers and daemon, plus `browser-use login`, an MCP server (`browser-use --cli-mcp`) and `browser-use skill install`. > > ```bash > uv tool install browser-use > browser-use <<'PY' > new_tab("https://example.com") > print(page_info()) > PY > ``` > > The `browser-harness` command keeps working. Domain skills and interaction skills stay in this repo. # Browser Harness ♞ Browser Harness lets Claude Code, Codex or Cursor use your real Chrome browser: open pages, click, type, read and download, logged in as you. Paste one prompt into your coding agent to set it up. It talks to Chrome over the DevTools Protocol (CDP), and the agent writes any missing helper as it works, so the harness gets better with each task. Open source, MIT licensed. Try browser-harness in [Browser Use Cloud](https://cloud.browser-use.com/v4?utm_campaign=browser-harness-use-in-cloud&utm_source=github) or paste the setup prompt into your coding agent. ``` ● agent: wants to upload a file │ ● agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py → helper missing │ ● agent writes it agent_helpers.py │ + custom helper ✓ file uploaded ``` **You will never use the browser again.** ## See it work **Task:** "Open my X profile, find my latest 20 video posts, and download them." [![Download my latest 20 X videos](docs/download-latest-20-x-videos.gif)](https://browser-use.com/showcase/videos/download-latest-20-x-videos.mp4) ## Setup prompt Paste into Claude Code or Codex (Cursor: use the [MCP config](#cursor) below): ```text Install browser-use with `uv tool install browser-use`, run `browser-use skill install` to register the skill, and connect it to my browser. If setup or connection fails, run `browser-use --doctor` and follow its output and the error message. ``` The agent will open `chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging`. On first setup, tick the checkbox so the agent can connect to your browser: ## How it works - [`install.md`](install.md) connects the agent to your browser. - [`SKILL.md`](SKILL.md) teaches it the browser workflow. - [`src/browser_harness/`](src/browser_harness/) stays protected while the agent writes reusable helpers in its local workspace. ## Compared with other browser tools | | Works with | Browser it drives | What you approve in your own Chrome | |---|---|---|---| | **Browser Harness** | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, any MCP client via `browser-harness-mcp` | Your running Chrome, logged in as you | Whole browser: on Chrome 144+, tick remote debugging in `chrome://inspect`, then click Allow | | **Playwright MCP** | Any MCP client (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot and more) | Its own browser profile by default. Your Chrome with `--extension` (Playwright Extension) or `--cdp-endpoint` | Chosen tabs (one tab group per client) via the extension, approval skippable with a token; or whole browser via `--cdp-endpoint` | | **Playwright CLI** | Claude Code, GitHub Copilot and other agents that run shell commands | Its own browser by default. Your Chrome with `attach --extension=chrome` or `attach --cdp=chrome` | Chosen tab via the Playwright Extension, or whole browser via `--cdp` | | **Chrome DevTools MCP** | Any MCP client (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Antigravity and more), plus a CLI | A new Chrome with a dedicated profile by default. Your Chrome 144+ with `--autoConnect` | Whole browser: the same Chrome 144+ toggle and Allow dialog; the server sees every open window of that profile | | **agent-browser** | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot and more, as a CLI with a skill, plus an MCP server | Its own Chrome for Testing by default. A copy of your Chrome profile with `--profile`. Your running Chrome with `--auto-connect` or `--cdp` | Whole browser via `--auto-connect` or `--cdp`: the same Chrome 144+ toggle and Allow dialog | | **Claude in Chrome** | Claude Code (CLI or VS Code) with the Claude extension, signed in with a direct Anthropic plan (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise), not an API key | Your Chrome, Edge or other Chromium browser, logged in as you | Per site: allow sites in the extension, or per action in Claude Code (auto mode can skip the per-site check). Claude works in a tab group it opens | | **ChatGPT Browser and browser extension** | Codex and ChatGPT chats in the ChatGPT desktop app, not Codex CLI or the Codex IDE extension | Browser: a separate profile. Extension: your Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera or Vivaldi profile | Per site: asks before each new website (allow once, for this site, or for all sites) | Matched eval by Browser Use on 100 of the 200 public [BU Bench V2.1](https://github.com/browser-use/benchmark) tasks (bu2-001 to bu2-100; 101-200 not run). Measured 2026-10-14. - Same agent for every tool: Codex CLI 0.144.6, GPT-6 Luna, medium reasoning, web search off. Same frozen judge. - Browser Harness was given to the agent as its CLI and SKILL.md, not `browser-harness-mcp`. Playwright MCP and Chrome DevTools MCP ran as MCP servers with default settings. agent-browser ran as its CLI and skill. - Every tool drove the same fresh Browser Use cloud browser over CDP. This does not measure each tool's default or local-Chrome mode. - One run per task. Agent failures were never retried. Runner, browser and judge failures were rerun once (Browser Harness 3 tasks, Playwright MCP 4, Chrome DevTools MCP 6, agent-browser 0). | Tool | Mean rubric score 0-100 (95% CI) | Fully solved | Median input tokens per task | Median model cost per task (GPT-6 Luna list price) | Median agent time per task | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Browser Harness a6426f84 (main) | 60.4 (55.2-65.4) | 11% | 2.1M | $0.042 | 9.0 min | | Playwright MCP 0.0.83 | 60.0 (55.1-65.0) | 11% | 4.4M | $0.066 | 8.3 min | | Chrome DevTools MCP 1.10.1 | 61.0 (55.8-65.9) | 11% | 6.7M | $0.097 | 8.7 min | | agent-browser 0.39.1 | 56.3 (51.1-61.5) | 9% | 3.3M | $0.056 | 11.2 min | No tool wins on score: every paired difference against Browser Harness has a 95% CI that includes zero (other tool minus Browser Harness: agent-browser -4.0, CI -10.0 to +1.8; Playwright MCP -0.4, -6.6 to +5.7; Chrome DevTools MCP +0.6, -5.6 to +6.6). Browser Harness had the lowest median input tokens (2.1M vs 3.3-6.7M) and the lowest median model cost ($0.042 vs $0.056-0.097). Model cost excludes browser, proxy and judge. It was slower than Playwright MCP and Chrome DevTools MCP (median 9.0 vs 8.3 and 8.7 min) and faster than agent-browser (11.2 min). These are medians, with no confidence intervals. A first agent-browser run was discarded: a setup bug on our side let it launch its own local browser instead of the shared cloud browser. The row shows the corrected rerun. Measured with Codex only. Claude Code, Cursor, Playwright CLI and Claude in Chrome were not measured. Method and per-task scores: [coding-agent-browser-tools.json](https://browser-use.com/benchmarks/coding-agent-browser-tools.json). ### When to use something else - **Playwright** (Test, MCP or CLI): isolated, repeatable CI tests of your own app, in a clean browser with no personal logins. - **Chrome DevTools MCP**: performance traces and DevTools debugging (network, console, source-mapped stack traces). - **Claude in Chrome**: you only use Claude and have a Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan. - **Cursor's built-in Browser**: the agent doesn't need your logged-in Chrome. It runs in its own per-workspace profile. OpenAI's Codex labels its browser feature "Browser use" in its settings. It is separate from Browser Use, the company behind this repo. ## Scale with Browser Use Cloud Use your local browser for logged-in, personal work. When you want many browsers in parallel, with live previews, proxies, stealth, CAPTCHA solving, and more, scale with [Browser Use Cloud](https://cloud.browser-use.com/new-api-key). ## MCP server `browser-use --cli-mcp` exposes the browser control helpers as MCP tools over stdio, so any MCP client (Claude Code, Devin, Cursor, etc.) can drive the browser without writing a second CDP layer. The older `browser-harness-mcp` keeps working; see [docs/MCP.md](docs/MCP.md). ### Cursor Add this to `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project, or to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project. It needs [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). ```json { "mcpServers": { "browser-use": { "type": "stdio", "command": "uvx", "args": ["browser-use", "--cli-mcp"] } } } ``` ## Contributing Bug fixes, documentation improvements, and agent-generated domain skills are welcome. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). --- [The Bitter Lesson of Agent Harnesses](https://browser-use.com/posts/bitter-lesson-agent-harnesses) · [Web Agents That Actually Learn](https://browser-use.com/posts/web-agents-that-actually-learn)
